# Storyboard: Chapter 7, The Counts Don’t Lie

*Generated by `tools/storyboard.mjs` from `app/story/ch07.js`. Do not edit by hand: change the story file and run `node tools/storyboard.mjs` again.*

## How to read this

Every screen of the game is one comic panel, called a frame. Frames are listed in reading order. Each one has:

- **Shot**: the storyboard, written for an illustrator (camera, who is where, what the moment feels like, where the lettering goes).
- **Scene**: what the game draws today, in plain words: the set, the camera, who is in shot and how, and any effects.
- **Captions**: the narration boxes, read first. **Balloons**: who speaks, in order. **Sound effect**: the big lettering. A line marked *(only if …)* shows only to a reader whose choices match.
- **Then**: what the reader does next (tap Next, choose, type, pick a look, count by twos, or do a Counts lesson).

Where the reader makes a choice, each option’s frames are grouped under a **Branch** heading, and the branches meet again at the frame named after them. `{name}` is the first part of her Clan name (Moon makes Moonpaw), `{petname}` is what her Tall One calls her, and `{they}`/`{them}`/`{their}` become she/her/her or he/him/his.

## The chapter

### f001 · panel 1

**Shot.** CLOSE-UP, BEFORE DAWN. Our cat sits bolt upright in its moss nest in the grey dark before sunrise, ears straight up, eyes wide, still half inside a dream; a small inset shows a wind chime turning on a high balcony. Its rows of bark stand along the mossy edge. Two captions, top left and at the bottom.

**Scene.** Den: the apprentices’ den under an enormous rosebush, at night. Camera: close on one nest (`nest`). Cast: you (sitting, full of wonder, in the nest, facing left). Also: clear weather; no moon; Riffle’s lucky stone in her nest, right where she put it (by her nose or under her chin, as she chose); her Case File along the mossy edge of her nest: a piece of bark for each card she holds, overlapping like roof tiles; her secret cards under the moss, a corner showing for each. Effects: night.

**Captions**

> You wake before the sun. A wind chime is still ringing in your ears, from your dream.
>
> Who was up there, awake, when the rain stopped? You know EXACTLY who.

**Then:** Next → f002.

**Then the Counts lesson** `ch07-pile` (pieces, prey in rows): 3 × 10 (lit a row at a time as it is asked; its own question, kept on its retry; a check: a right one never makes the fact hard). None of this frame’s own lines is said again over the first question: it is asked in its own words, and as a check it is never timed. She types each answer on the keypad; a miss gets the count scratched in the earth, and comes back two questions later (the questions in between come from `ch04-tens`, the easiest first, never a pair asked already while there is another, each asked as this lesson’s own question, in its picture and its voice after “An easy one.”). On to f015.

- Asking 3 × 10:
  - *Caption*: Three front rows of ten. How many pieces?
- Asking 3 × 10 again after a miss:
  - **Tallyheart**: “Here’s that one again.”
  - *Caption*: Three front rows of ten. How many pieces?
- After a miss that doesn’t end in a zero: “Remember: counting by tens, every number ends in a zero. Let’s scratch it out: ten marks for every row.”
- No closing line: the next frame goes straight on.

### f100 · panel 97

**Shot.** WIDE, INSIDE THE DEN, NIGHT, THE TAP PICTURE. The grey apprentice and our cat both puff out their cheeks as round as they will go, which is very silly, and try not to laugh. In play the counting picture takes the panel: his face and hers close up side by side, cheeks puffed, the next cheek glowing; each tap lights its six whiskers and puts the next number in our cat’s balloon, 6, 12, 18, 24. One caption at the top.

**Scene.** Den: the apprentices’ den under an enormous rosebush, at night. Camera: inside the den (`inside`). Cast: the snoring apprentice (sitting, happy, in a nest, left, facing right); you (sitting, happy, in the nest, facing left). **Captions**

> He puffs out his cheeks. You puff out yours.

**Then she counts by 6s on the cheeks** (the skip-count): four cheeks close up in a row, six whiskers on each, three on top and three below (left to right: the face of the snoring apprentice, its two cheeks puffed round; your face, its two cheeks puffed round); 4 taps, one on each cheek in turn (the next one glows; a tap anywhere else makes it wiggle), each lighting its whiskers, top row then bottom, and adding its running total under it and in her own balloon: 6, 12, 18, 24. ## The Case File’s cards

A piece of bark for each thing she finds out: one picture scratched in, one line, and a mark in a corner (an eye for what she saw herself, an ear for what she was only told). Each goes into her Case File at the panel that gives it, in this order:

| Card | Mark | Its line | Given at | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `waffles-no-moon` | ear | Waffles says there was NO moon on the storm night. | f011 | drawn touching `fox-moon` from the moment she holds both: “Two say no moon. Only the fox says moon.” |
| `my-count` | eye | My count: twenty-four gone in six nights. A dragon would take sixty. | f040, f056 |  |
| `prints-sprinkle` | eye | Sprinkle’s prints are huge. The thief’s are tiny. | f064 |  |
| `tunnel` | eye | A tunnel under the back of the pile, too small for a dragon. | f086 | drawn touching `coil-diggers` from the moment she holds both: “Coil felt them. Now I’ve seen where.” |

## The book page

Title: *{name}paw’s First Moon*. This chapter’s page, under “Chapter 7: The Counts Don’t Lie”. Lines shown when their condition matches the reader’s choices:

- (always) Before the sun was up, {name}paw asked Princess Waffles about the storm night. NO moon, she said, not a sliver: two witnesses against one fox.
- (always) At the sixth morning count, four more pieces were gone, though eighteen guards had watched all night: twenty-four in six nights.
- (always) Tallyheart taught {name}paw {their} seventh Count, whiskers: the sixes.
- (if ch3Told is true) Then {name}paw and Tallyheart worked it out: four a night for six nights is twenty-four, but a dragon who eats ten fish a meal would have taken sixty.
- (if ch3Told is false or not set) Then {name}paw and Tallyheart counted twenty-four in six nights, and Riffle helped {name}paw work out that a dragon who eats ten fish a meal would have taken sixty.
- (always) Under the Old Bridge, Sprinkle’s prints were huge; the thief’s, in the marsh, were tiny. Sprinkle tried to fly, and couldn’t, so Reynard’s story that the dragon FLEW can’t be true.
- (if ch3Told is true) At dusk, behind the back row, {name}paw and Tallyheart found the mouth of a tunnel under the bramble roots, much too small for a dragon.
- (if ch3Told is false or not set) At dusk, behind the back row, {name}paw found the mouth of a tunnel under the bramble roots, much too small for a dragon.
- (always) That night, the grey tom and {name}paw counted their whiskers: twenty-four, between them.
- (no dream typed) {name}paw’s dream that night went uncounted.
